tasks.title: Silent frame-of-reference error
tasks.answer:
## TL;DR  
The most common reason that **only the off‑diagonal Mueller element S₁₂ disagrees while S₁₁ is identical** is a **different sign / basis convention** in the way the two codes translate the complex amplitude scattering functions ( S₁, S₂ ) into the Mueller matrix.  In practice this can be caused by:

| Category | Typical culprit | How it shows up in the output |
|----------|----------------|------------------------------|
| **Polarisation basis** | “parallel / perpendicular” (‖/⊥) vs “horizontal / vertical” (H/V) or a 90° rotation of the reference plane | S₁₂ changes sign (and often magnitude) because Q is defined opposite |
| **Scattering‑plane definition** | Azimuth φ measured from the incident plane vs from the detector plane, or using φ → 180°‑φ | S₁₂ → –S₁₂ |
| **Mueller‑matrix convention** | Chandrasekhar vs Bohren‑Huffman vs IAU vs IEC | The sign of S₁₂ (and S₁₃, S₁₄) is flipped |
| **Complex‑refractive‑index sign** | n = n + ik vs n = n – ik (or different sign in the wave‑vector) | S₁₂ (and S₁₁) can change sign; S₁₁ staying the same points to a sign that only affects the cross‑term |
| **Phase reference** | Electric‑field phase taken as e^{+ik·r} vs e^{-ik·r} | S₁₂ sign flips, S₁₁ unchanged |
| **Stokes‑vector ordering** | (I,Q,U,V) vs (I,‑Q,U,V) or (I,V,U,Q) | S₁₂ sign changes |
| **Numerical/implementation bug** | Missing “‑” in the formula for S₁₂, array‑index mix‑up, single‑precision overflow | Could give a different magnitude as well as sign |

Because S₁₁ matches to the last digit, the size parameter, refractive index, wavelength, and the core Mie‑algorithm are *identical* in both programs.  The discrepancy is therefore almost certainly a **convention mismatch** rather than a physics error.

Below is a systematic checklist you can run through to pinpoint the exact cause.

---

## 1. Verify the “raw” amplitude scattering functions

Both Mie codes compute the complex amplitude functions **S₁(θ)** and **S₂(θ)** (often called *S1* and *S2*).  The Mueller matrix elements are built from them:

\[
\begin{aligned}
S_{11} &= \tfrac12\bigl(|S_1|^2+|S_2|^2\bigr)\\[4pt]
S_{12} &= \tfrac12\bigl(|S_2|^2-|S_1|^2\bigr)\\[4pt]
S_{33} &= \Re\{S_1 S_2^{*}\}\\[4pt]
S_{34} &= \Im\{S_1 S_2^{*}\}
\end{aligned}
\]

(Other conventions differ by a sign in front of the second term of S₁₂, or by swapping S₁↔S₂.)

**What to do**

1. **Print S₁ and S₂** (real & imag) from both programs at θ = 90°.  
2. Compute S₁₁ and S₁₂ *by hand* using the formula you expect.  
3. Compare the hand‑computed values with the program outputs.

If the hand‑computed S₁₁ matches both programs but the hand‑computed S₁₂ matches only one, the mismatch is in the *conversion* from S₁,S₂ to the Mueller matrix.

---

## 2. Check the definition of the Stokes vector

| Convention | Q sign | U sign | V sign |
|------------|--------|--------|--------|
| **IAU / Chandrasekhar** | Q = I_‖ − I_⊥ | U = I_{45°} − I_{‑45°} | V = I_R − I_L |
| **Bohren‑Huffman** | Q = I_⊥ − I_‖ (opposite) | same | same |
| **IEC** | Q = I_H − I_V | U = I_{+45°} − I_{‑45°} | V = I_R − I_L |

If one code uses the IAU definition and the other the Bohren‑Huffman definition, **S₁₂ will be opposite in sign** (because S₁₂ multiplies Q).  The magnitude can also differ if the code also swaps the order of the perpendicular/parallel components in the amplitude functions.

**What to do**

* Look at the documentation or source for each program and locate the routine that builds the Mueller matrix.  
* Verify which Stokes ordering (I,Q,U,V) and which sign convention for Q is used.  
* If they differ, you can either (a) change one program’s convention, or (b) apply a sign flip to the offending element when comparing.

---

## 3. Scattering‑plane vs laboratory‑plane reference

The Mueller matrix is defined with respect to a **reference plane** (the plane containing the incident and scattered directions).  Some codes define the *parallel* direction as the component **in the scattering plane**, others as **perpendicular to the scattering plane**.  A 90° rotation of the reference plane changes the sign of S₁₂ (and also S₁₃, S₁₄).

**What to do**

* Confirm the definition of the *parallel* (‖) and *perpendicular* (⊥) polarisation vectors in each code.  
* For a sphere the scattering is symmetric, but the sign of S₁₂ still depends on which vector you call “parallel”.  
* If one code uses the *laboratory* plane (incident‑polarisation plane) and the other the *scattering* plane, you will see exactly the sign flip you observe.

---

## 4. Complex‑refractive‑index sign convention

Mie theory can be written with the time‑dependence **e^{−iωt}** (most physics texts) or **e^{+iωt}** (some engineering texts).  This choice flips the sign of the imaginary part of the refractive index **k** and consequently the sign of the phase of the scattering amplitudes.  For a sphere the intensity (S₁₁) is unchanged, but the cross‑terms (S₁₂, S₃₃, S₃₄) can change sign.

**What to do**

* Print the complex refractive index that each program receives.  
* Verify that both use the same sign for the imaginary part (e.g., n = 1.5 + 0.01i).  
* If one uses n = 1.5 − 0.01i, the sign of S₁₂ will be reversed.

---

## 5. Phase‑reference (e^{±ik·r}) and sign of the wave‑vector

Related to the previous point, some codes adopt **e^{+ik·r}** for the incident field while others use **e^{−ik·r}**.  This again flips the sign of the *cross* terms without affecting the total intensity.

**What to do**

* Look at the definition of the incident field in the source.  
* If you find a different sign in the exponential, you have identified the source of the sign change.

---

## 6. Numerical precision / rounding

The numbers you quoted are on the order of 10⁻¹³, i.e. close to the double‑precision limit for a quantity that results from subtracting two nearly equal large numbers.  A single‑precision implementation could easily produce a different sign for the small difference.

**What to do**

* Check whether both programs are compiled/run in **double precision**.  
* If one is single‑precision, re‑run it in double precision and see whether S₁₂ moves toward the other value.  
* Compare the *intermediate* quantities (|S₁|², |S₂|²) – if they differ by a few parts in 10⁶, the subtraction that yields S₁₂ can flip sign.

---

## 7. Verify the input parameters are truly identical

Even a tiny mismatch in radius, wavelength, or refractive index can change the phase of the scattering amplitudes enough to flip S₁₂ while leaving S₁₁ essentially unchanged.

**What to do**

* Print the **size parameter** \(x = 2\pi r / \lambda\) that each code actually uses.  
* Print the **real and imaginary parts** of the refractive index as read by each program.  
* Ensure the wavelength is interpreted the same way (vacuum vs medium).  

---

## 8. Look for a coding bug

If the documentation and conventions all line up, the discrepancy may be a simple sign error in the implementation.

Typical places where a “‑” can be lost:

| Location | Typical line (pseudo‑code) |
|----------|----------------------------|
| Building S₁₂ from | `S12 = 0.5*(absS2*absS2 - absS1*absS1);` (should be `absS1*absS1 - absS2*absS2` for some conventions) |
| Swapping S₁ ↔ S₂ | `S12 = 0.5*(absS1*absS1 - absS2*absS2);` (if S₁ and S₂ are interchanged) |
| Using `real(S1*S2)` vs `real(S2*S1)` (no effect) but using `imag` with wrong sign |
| Indexing of the Mueller matrix (row‑major vs column‑major) |

**What to do**

* Search the source for the routine that fills the Mueller matrix.  
* Compare it line‑by‑line with a reference implementation (e.g., the classic BHMIE code).  
* Add a unit test that feeds a known analytic case (e.g., Rayleigh scattering of a tiny sphere) where the exact S₁₂ is known (it should be zero for a perfect sphere in the Rayleigh limit).  

---

## 9. Quick sanity check with a known analytic limit

For a **Rayleigh‑size sphere** (size parameter ≪ 1) the scattering matrix reduces to

\[
S_{11}=1,\qquad S_{12}= \frac{1}{2}\bigl(1- \cos^{2}\theta\bigr),\qquad S_{33}=S_{44}=0,
\]

or, depending on the convention, \(S_{12}= -\frac{1}{2}(1-\cos^{2}\theta)\).  At θ = 90° the magnitude is 0.5, and the sign is the only difference between conventions.  Run both programs with a radius of, say, 10 nm at 550 nm (size parameter ≈ 0.11) and see which sign each returns.  This will immediately reveal which convention each code follows.

---

## 10. Summary checklist (what to **check first**)

| Step | Action | Expected outcome if the problem is a convention mismatch |
|------|--------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| 1 | Print S₁, S₂ from both codes | They should be identical (or complex‑conjugates) |
| 2 | Compute S₁₁, S₁₂ manually | Manual S₁₁ matches both; manual S₁₂ matches **one** of them |
| 3 | Look at the Mueller‑matrix routine | Identify the sign used in the S₁₂ formula |
| 4 | Verify Stokes‑vector definition (Q sign) | If one uses opposite Q, flip sign of S₁₂ to reconcile |
| 5 | Verify reference plane (‖/⊥) | If they differ, a 90° rotation will flip S₁₂ |
| 6 | Check refractive‑index sign & e^{±ik·r} | Opposite sign will also flip S₁₂ |
| 7 | Confirm double precision | If single precision, re‑run in double and compare |
| 8 | Run a Rayleigh‑limit test | The sign that survives is the convention of the code |

---

## Bottom line

The **most probable cause** is a **different sign convention for the Stokes Q component (or for the parallel/perpendicular basis)**, which directly flips the sign of S₁₂ while leaving S₁₁ untouched.  A secondary possibility is a different **phase convention** (e^{±ik·r}) or **refractive‑index sign**.  By printing the raw amplitude functions, checking the Stokes‑vector definition, and confirming the reference plane, you can pinpoint the exact mismatch and either adjust one program’s output or change its source to use the same convention as the other.

A bug in the part of the code that builds the scattering matrix from the Mie amplitudes (e.g. swapping S₁ and S₂, using the wrong complex‑conjugate, or applying a different normalisation) will produce exactly the pattern you see: the total intensity (S₁₁) is unchanged, but the polarisation‑cross term changes sign and magnitude.

## 1.  Understand how the scattering matrix is built in Mie theory  

For a single sphere the 4×4 Mueller matrix reduces to four independent elements (the rest are zero by symmetry).  
In the usual **Bohren‑Huffman / Mishchenko** convention the elements are expressed through the two complex scattering amplitudes **S₁(θ)** and **S₂(θ)**:

| Element | Formula (Mishchenko) |
|---------|----------------------|
| **S₁₁** | \(\displaystyle \frac{|S_1|^2+|S_2|^2}{2}\) |
| **S₁₂** | \(\displaystyle \frac{|S_2|^2-|S_1|^2}{2}\) |
| **S₃₃** | \(\displaystyle \Re\{S_1 S_2^{*}\}\) |
| **S₃₄** | \(\displaystyle \Im\{S_1 S_2^{*}\}\) |

All other Mueller elements are zero for a sphere.  
**Key point:** *Only the relative ordering of |S₁| and |S₂| determines the sign of S₁₂.* If a program swaps the two amplitudes, or uses a different definition of the amplitudes (e.g. S₁↔S₂, or S₁→−S₁), S₁₁ stays the same (it is symmetric in |S₁|² and |S₂|²) while S₁₂ flips sign and can change magnitude if the amplitudes are not exactly equal.

1. **Print the raw scattering amplitudes**  
   ```text
   Program A:  S1 = a + ib,   S2 = c + id
   Program B:  S1 = a' + ib', S2 = c' + id'
   ```
   Then compute:
   ```text
   S11_A = (|S1|^2 + |S2|^2)/2
   S12_A = (|S2|^2 - |S1|^2)/2
   ```
   Do the same for B.  
   If the amplitudes are identical (within round‑off) but the *order* of the two amplitudes is swapped, you have found the culprit.

2. **Swap the amplitudes in one program**  
   In Program B, exchange the variables that hold S₁ and S₂ before the Mueller‑matrix construction. If the new S₁₂ matches Program A, the issue is a convention mismatch.

3. **Check the sign of the imaginary part of the refractive index**  
   For a weakly absorbing sphere the two amplitudes are almost equal; a sign error in *k* can make |S₂| > |S₁| in one code and the opposite in the other.

4. **Run a sanity test with a Rayleigh scatterer**  
   Choose a radius ≪ λ (e.g. 10 nm) and a real refractive index. In the Rayleigh limit the analytical expressions give:
   \[
   S_{12} = \frac{1}{2}\bigl(|S_2|^2 - |S_1|^2\bigr) = \frac{1}{2}\bigl(\cos^2\theta - 1\bigr) \times \text{const}
   \]
   The sign is known analytically. Compare both programs to the analytic value; the one that deviates is the one using a different convention.

5. **Inspect the source code**  
   Look for the line that builds the Mueller matrix. Typical snippets:
   ```c
   S11 = 0.5*(cabs(S1)*cabs(S1) + cabs(S2)*cabs(S2));
   S12 = 0.5*(cabs(S2)*cabs(S2) - cabs(S1)*cabs(S1));
   ```
   If you see the terms reversed, you have identified the sign error.

6. **Check the output format**  
   Some libraries output the matrix as:
   ```
   [S11 S12 S33 S34]
   ```
   while others output:
   ```
   [S11 S12 S34 S33]
   ```
   Mis‑reading the file can make you think S₁₂ is wrong when you are actually looking at S₃₃ or S₃₄.

---

## 4.  Typical “gotchas” that produce exactly the pattern you observed

| Gotcha | Effect on S₁₁ | Effect on S₁₂ | How it arises |
|--------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| **Swapped amplitudes (S₁ ↔ S₂)** | unchanged (symmetrical) | sign flips, magnitude changes if |S₁|≠|S₂| | Different definition of “parallel” vs “perpendicular” polarisation |
| **Opposite sign in the definition of S₁₂** | unchanged | sign flips (|S₁|≈|S₂| → small value) | Typo in the formula |
| **Different scattering‑plane orientation** (θ → 180°–θ) | unchanged (|S₁|²+|S₂|² symmetric) | sign flips because |S₁| and |S₂| exchange roles at 90° | Some codes define θ from the *backward* direction |
| **Using e^{+iωt} vs e^{-iωt}** | unchanged (intensity) | sign may change if the code uses `S1*S2` instead of `S1*conj(S2)` | Phase convention |
| **Normalization to extinction vs. scattering cross‑section** | may change overall scale but often forced to 1 at θ=0° | can change magnitude of S₁₂ while S₁₁ stays matched (if both are later renormalised) | Different libraries have different default normalisations |
| **Stokes ordering mismatch** | unchanged (still I) | you may be reading the wrong element (e.g. reading S₃₃ as S₁₂) | Output file format confusion |

---

## 5.  What to do after you locate the source

1. **Document the convention** used by each program (e.g. “Program A follows Mishchenko’s definition: S₁ = S⊥, S₂ = S∥, θ measured from forward direction”).  
2. **If you need the results in a common convention**, either:
   * Convert the matrix after the fact (swap S₁ and S₂, change sign of S₁₂, etc.), or  
   * Modify the source of one program to adopt the other convention (usually a one‑line change).  
3. **Add a sanity‑check routine** to your workflow that prints the size parameter, the two amplitudes, and the four non‑zero Mueller elements for a few benchmark angles (0°, 45°, 90°). This will catch future mismatches early.  
4. **Consider unit tests**: compare against the analytical Rayleigh solution for a tiny sphere and against a published Mie‑code reference (e.g. BHMIE) for a set of size parameters.

---

## 6.  Quick “cheat‑sheet” for the most common fix

| Symptom | Likely cause | One‑line fix (pseudo‑code) |
|---------|--------------|----------------------------|
| S₁₂ has opposite sign, same magnitude | Swapped S₁ ↔ S₂ | `tmp = S1; S1 = S2; S2 = tmp;` |
| S₁₂ sign wrong, magnitude ≈ ¼ of expected | Wrong formula (`|S1|² - |S2|²`) | `S12 = 0.5*(cabs(S2)*cabs(S2) - cabs(S1)*cabs(S1));` |
| S₁₂ ≈ 0 while S₁₁ correct | Using forward‑scattering angle (θ=0) where |S₁|=|S₂| | Test at θ=90° or 45° |
| S₁₂ magnitude differs by a constant factor | Different normalisation (e.g. divide by C_sca) | Multiply/divide by the same factor used in the other code |

---

## 7.  Bottom line

The discrepancy is almost certainly **not a physical error** (the particle, wavelength, and size are identical) but a **difference in how the two programs translate the underlying Mie amplitudes into the Mueller matrix**. By systematically checking the items in the checklist—especially the **ordering of the amplitudes, the definition of the scattering angle, and the polarisation basis**—you will pinpoint the exact convention mismatch or bug. Once identified, either adjust the code or apply a post‑processing conversion so that both programs speak the same “language”.  

Good luck, and happy debugging!

## TL;DR  
The two codes are using **different conventions** for the *off‑diagonal* Mueller element S₁₂ (or for the underlying amplitude matrix) while they agree on the *intensity* element S₁₁.  The most common culprits are:

| Category | What can change the sign of S₁₂ (or make it look “different”) |
|----------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Reference‑plane / azimuth definition** | Scattering plane defined with opposite azimuth (φ → –φ) or with the incident beam taken as +z vs –z. |
| **Polarisation basis** | (eθ , eφ) vs (e⊥ , e∥) or a 90° rotation of the basis vectors. |
| **Stokes‑vector ordering / Q‑sign** | Some codes define **Q** = I∥ – I⊥, others Q = I⊥ – I∥. |
| **Mueller‑matrix vs amplitude‑matrix sign conventions** | S₁₂ = –Re(S₁S₂*) in one textbook, +Re(S₁S₂*) in another. |
| **Complex‑conjugation convention** | Using S₂* instead of S₂ (or vice‑versa) when forming the Mueller elements. |
| **Normalization / scaling** | Division by k², by the geometric cross‑section, or by the total scattering cross‑section can flip the sign of the *real* part if a minus sign is hidden in the definition. |
| **Coordinate‑system handedness** | Right‑handed vs left‑handed (or a mirror transformation) changes the sign of the azimuthal basis vector and therefore S₁₂. |
| **Numerical precision / rounding** | S₁₂ is ~10⁻¹³, i.e. three orders of magnitude smaller than S₁₁; a single‑precision implementation can easily change its sign through round‑off. |
| **Input mismatch that only affects the phase** | A different surrounding‑medium index, a different sign for the complex refractive index, or a different size‑parameter definition (2πr/λ in vacuum vs in medium) changes the phase of the Mie coefficients and can flip the sign of the interference term that produces S₁₂. |

Below is a **check‑list** you can run through systematically to pinpoint the source of the discrepancy.

---

## 1. Verify the *exact* definitions used by each program  

| Item | What to look for | Why it matters |
|------|------------------|----------------|
| **Mueller‑matrix element formula** | Is S₁₂ = –Re(S₁ S₂*) or +Re(S₁ S₂*)?  (or is it –Im(...)?). | The sign of the real‑part term is the most common source of a sign flip. |
| **Stokes vector convention** | Does the code use (I, Q, U, V) with Q = I∥ – I⊥ or Q = I⊥ – I∥? | Changing the sign of Q flips the sign of every element that couples to Q, i.e. S₁₂, S₂₁, S₂₂, S₃₄, … |
| **Polarisation basis** | Are the basis vectors (eθ, eφ) or (e⊥, e∥) and which one is “horizontal”? | Rotating the basis by 90° changes the sign of the cross‑terms. |
| **Scattering‑plane azimuth** | Is the azimuth φ measured clockwise or counter‑clockwise? | A reversal of φ → –φ changes the sign of the sin φ term that appears in S₁₂. |
| **Reference direction for Q** | Is the “horizontal” direction taken along the scattering plane or perpendicular to it? | Same effect as the Q‑sign issue. |
| **Normalization** | Is the matrix normalized to the *total* scattering cross‑section, to the *geometric* cross‑section, or left un‑scaled? | A hidden factor of –1 can be introduced when the authors define the normalized matrix as –S/σ. |
| **Complex‑conjugation rule** | When forming the Mueller elements, does the code use S₁ S₂* or S₁* S₂? | Swapping the conjugate flips the sign of the real part. |
| **Handedness of the coordinate system** | Right‑handed (x × y = z) or left‑handed? | A mirror transformation flips the sign of the azimuthal basis vector, again flipping S₁₂. |

**Action:** Print (or log) the intermediate amplitude matrix elements (S₁, S₂, S₃, S₄) from each code for the same angle. Compare them directly. If they differ only by a sign in S₂ (or S₃), you have found the culprit.

---

## 2. Check the *input* parameters that affect phase only  

| Parameter | How it could affect S₁₂ | What to verify |
|-----------|------------------------|----------------|
| **Refractive index of the surrounding medium** | The size parameter is x = 2π r nₘ/λ.  Using nₘ = 1 (air) vs nₘ = 1.33 (water) changes the phase of the Mie coefficients, which can flip the sign of the interference term that produces S₁₂. | Print the *size parameter* that each code computes. |
| **Complex refractive index of the particle** | A sign error in the imaginary part (e.g., using n = nᵣ – i nᵢ instead of nᵣ + i nᵢ) changes the phase of the coefficients. | Verify that both codes read the same complex number (e.g., 1.5+0.01i). |
| **Wavelength definition** | Some codes take λ in vacuum, others in the surrounding medium (λₘ = λ₀ / nₘ). | Confirm that the wavelength passed to each code is the same physical quantity. |
| **Radius** | Same as above – ensure the radius is not being interpreted as a diameter or as a volume‑equivalent sphere. | Print the *size parameter* x = 2π r/λ used internally. |
| **Angle definition** | θ = 0° = forward scattering in one code, θ = 180° = forward in another. | Verify that the “90°” you passed is interpreted the same way. |
| **Polarisation of the incident beam** | Some codes assume the incident electric field is polarized parallel to the scattering plane; others assume perpendicular. | Check the documentation or source for the default incident polarisation. |

**Action:** Run a *sanity test* where you set the refractive index to a purely real value (no absorption) and the surrounding medium to n = 1.0. In that case the analytical Mie solution for a sphere gives S₁₂ = 0 at 90° for many size parameters. If one code still returns a non‑zero value, the problem is definitely a convention issue rather than an input mismatch.

---

## 3. Examine the *numerical* implementation  

| Issue | Why it can matter for a ~10⁻¹³ element | What to do |
|-------|----------------------------------------|------------|
| **Single‑ vs double‑precision arithmetic** | S₁₂ is three orders of magnitude smaller than S₁₁; rounding errors in single precision (≈7 decimal digits) can change its sign. | Force both codes to use double precision (or higher) and re‑run. |
| **Series truncation (n‑max)** | If the series is truncated too early, the higher‑order terms that contribute to the cross‑terms may be missing, leading to an inaccurate sign. | Compare the n‑max used (often `nmax ≈ x + 4x^(1/3) + 2`). Increase it and see if S₁₂ stabilises. |
| **Recurrence‑relation stability** | The Riccati‑Bessel functions (ψₙ, ξₙ) are computed via upward/downward recursions; an unstable recursion can introduce a phase error. | Swap to a different Bessel‑function routine (e.g., use `scipy.special.spherical_jn` vs a custom routine) and compare. |
| **Complex‑number handling** | Some languages (e.g., Fortran) treat `-0.0` differently from `+0.0`; a sign can be lost when converting to real‑valued Mueller elements. | Print the raw complex values before taking the real part. |
| **Rounding when writing output** | The printed value may be rounded to 5‑6 significant figures; a value of –1.8e‑13 could be displayed as –1.8e‑13 in one program and +4.1e‑14 in another if the underlying value is actually –4.1e‑14 but rounded differently. | Output with full double‑precision (`%.17e`) and compare. |

**Action:** Run both programs with a *high‑precision* (e.g., 128‑bit) library (MPFR, mpmath) for a single angle. If the sign converges to the same value, the discrepancy is purely numerical; if not, it is a convention issue.

---

## 4. Cross‑check with an *independent* reference  

1. **Analytical Mie code** – e.g., Bohren & Huffman’s `bhmie` (Fortran) or the Python `miepython` package. Compute S₁₁ and S₁₂ at 90° for the exact same size parameter and refractive index.  
2. **Commercial / benchmark software** – e.g., DDSCAT, MiePlot, or the T‑matrix code `scattnlay`.  
3. **Hand‑calculated low‑order case** – For a very small particle (Rayleigh limit, x ≪ 1) the Mueller matrix is known analytically:  

   \[
   S_{11}=1,\qquad S_{12}= \frac{1-\cos^{2}\theta}{1+\cos^{2}\theta}\,,
   \]

   (or a similar simple expression depending on the convention). Plug θ = 90°; you should get S₁₂ = 0.  If the two programs give opposite signs, the sign convention is the issue.

**Action:** Compare the three results. If the independent code matches Program A, then Program B is using a different convention (or vice‑versa). If the independent code matches neither, you have a bug in both or a hidden input mismatch.

---

## 5. Practical “quick‑diagnostic” script  

```python
# pseudo‑Python, works for most Mie libraries
import numpy as np
from miepython import mie

# ---- user inputs (identical for both runs) ----
lam   = 550e-9          # vacuum wavelength [m]
r     = 100e-9          # radius [m]
m     = 1.5 + 0.01j     # particle refractive index
n_med = 1.0             # surrounding medium

# ---- derived size parameter ----
x = 2*np.pi*r*n_med/lam

# ---- compute amplitude functions S1, S2 ----
S1, S2, S3, S4 = mie(m, x)   # returns complex amplitude matrix

# ---- Mueller elements at a given scattering angle theta ----
theta = np.pi/2   # 90 deg
# amplitude functions are already angle‑dependent in many libraries;
# if not, evaluate the series manually for the chosen theta.

# Example conversion (Bohren & Huffman):
S11 = 0.5*(np.abs(S1)**2 + np.abs(S2)**2)
S12 = 0.5*(np.abs(S2)**2 - np.abs(S1)**2)   # note the sign!

print(f"S11 = {S11:.5e}, S12 = {S12:.5e}")
```

Run the same script with the two *different* conversion formulas for S₁₂ (the one with a minus sign and the one with a plus sign). The output will reproduce exactly the two numbers you observed, confirming that the sign comes from the conversion formula.

---

## 6. Summary checklist  

| Step | What to do | Expected outcome if the problem is a convention mismatch |
|------|------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| **A. Print raw amplitude matrix** | Output S₁, S₂, S₃, S₄ (complex) from both codes. | They should be identical (or complex‑conjugates). |
| **B. Verify Stokes‑vector definition** | Check documentation or source for the Q‑sign. | One code will have Q → –Q relative to the other. |
| **C. Confirm scattering‑plane orientation** | Print the azimuth φ used internally. | One code will have φ → –φ. |
| **D. Test a Rayleigh‑limit case** | Use x ≪ 1, where analytic S₁₂ = 0. | Both codes should give ~0; if one gives a non‑zero sign, it’s a convention. |
| **E. Force double precision** | Compile/run both with `-fdefault-real-8` (Fortran) or `-DDOUBLE` (C). | Sign should stay the same; magnitude may change slightly. |
| **F. Compare with a third reference** | Run a known‑good Mie implementation. | The third result will match one of the two; the other is the outlier. |
| **G. Check input parsing** | Print the *exact* size parameter, refractive index, wavelength used. | Any mismatch will be obvious. |
| **H. Look for hidden minus signs** | Search source for `-` before `S12` or before `Q`. | You’ll find the line that flips the sign. |

---

## 7. What to do once you have identified the cause  

*If it is a convention issue* – decide which convention you need for downstream processing and either (i) modify the code that produces the “wrong” sign, or (ii) apply a post‑processing sign flip (`S12 → -S12`) together with the corresponding flips for S₂₁, S₂₂, S₃₄, S₄₃, etc.

*If it is a numerical precision issue* – switch both codes to double (or higher) precision, increase the truncation order, and verify convergence of S₁₂ with respect to `nmax`.

*If it is an input‑mismatch* – correct the way the size parameter or wavelength is computed (e.g., always use λ in the surrounding medium) and re‑run.

*If it is a bug* – file a bug report with a minimal reproducible example (the radius, refractive index, wavelength, and angle that give the sign flip). Include the printed amplitude matrix so the maintainer can see the exact point of divergence.

---

## Bottom line  

The **exact match of S₁₁** tells you that the *size parameter* and the *overall scattering efficiency* are being computed identically. The **sign discrepancy in S₁₂** almost always stems from a *different definition* of either the Stokes Q‑parameter, the scattering‑plane azimuth, or the way the amplitude matrix is turned into Mueller elements. By printing the intermediate complex amplitudes, checking the Stokes‑vector conventions, and comparing with a third, trusted implementation, you can pinpoint the source in a few minutes. Once the convention is aligned (or the sign is deliberately flipped), the two programs will agree.

**Step 1 –  Write a simple model for the run time**

For a program that can be split into a *serial* part (that must run on one core) and a *parallel* part (that can be divided among the cores) Amdahl’s law gives  

\[
T(N)=T_{\text{serial}}+\frac{T_{\text{parallel}}}{N},
\]

where  

* \(T(N)\) – measured wall‑clock time when the job uses \(N\) cores,  
* \(T_{\text{serial}}\) – time that cannot be parallelised (the same for any \(N\)),  
* \(T_{\text{parallel}}\) – the time the parallel part would take on a single core.

The model is linear in the variable \(1/N\); we can determine the two unknowns from the measurements.

---

**Step 2 –  Solve for the two parameters**

Take the first two data points (they are the most reliable because the later points start to feel other overheads).

\[
\begin{cases}
T_{\text{serial}}+\dfrac{T_{\text{parallel}}}{3}=412\\[4pt]
T_{\text{serial}}+\dfrac{T_{\text{parallel}}}{6}=208
\end{cases}
\]

Subtract the second equation from the first:

\[
\frac{T_{\text{parallel}}}{3}-\frac{T_{\text{parallel}}}{6}=204
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{T_{\text{parallel}}}{6}=204
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
T_{\text{parallel}}=1224\;\text{s}.
\]

Insert this value back into one of the equations:

\[
T_{\text{serial}} = 208-\frac{1224}{6}=208-204=4\;\text{s}.
\]

So the model that fits the first three measurements almost perfectly is  

\[
\boxed{T(N)=4\;+\;\frac{1224}{N}\;\text{seconds}}.
\]

(If we also include the fourth point (12 cores) in a least‑squares fit we obtain a slightly larger serial term, about 12 s, but the trend is the same.)

---

**Step 3 –  Predict the time on 256 cores**

\[
\begin{aligned}
T(256) &= 4 + \frac{1224}{256}\\[4pt]
       &= 4 + 4.78125\\[4pt]
       &\approx 8.8\;\text{s}.
\end{aligned}
\]

---

### Result

**The same run on 256 cores would be expected to finish in roughly 9 seconds** (≈ 8.8 s).  

---

### Remarks / Caveats

* The estimate assumes the only limitation is the serial fraction (≈ 0.3 % of the total work).  
* Real systems often show additional overheads (communication, scheduling, memory‑bandwidth limits) that become noticeable at very high core counts; therefore the actual time could be a little larger (perhaps 10–12 s).  
* Using all four data points in a linear regression gives a slightly more conservative prediction of about **17 s**; the true value is expected to lie between the two estimates, with the Amdahl‑law value (≈ 9 s) being the most common textbook answer.

The run‑time \(T\) does not fall exactly in proportion to the number of cores \(N\); there is a small serial part (overhead, I/O, …) that limits the speed‑up.  
A convenient way to model this is **Amdahl’s law**

\[
T(N)=T_{1}\Bigl[(1-p)+\frac{p}{N}\Bigr],
\]

where  

* \(T_{1}\) – the time the program would take on a single core,  
* \(p\) – the fraction of the work that can be parallelised ( \(0\le p\le 1\) ).

If we rewrite the formula

\[
T(N)=A + B\frac{1}{N},
\qquad\text{with }A=T_{1}(1-p),\; B=T_{1}p,
\]

the relationship becomes a straight line when we plot the measured times versus \(1/N\).

---

### 2.  Fit the line to the four measurements  

| Run | Cores \(N\) | Time \(T\) (s) | \(1/N\) |
|-----|------------|----------------|--------|

| 2   | 6          | 208            | 0.16667 |

| 4   | 12         | 118            | 0.08333 |

\boxed{A \approx 12.5\ \text{s}},\qquad
\boxed{B \approx 1.19\times10^{3}\ \text{s}} .
\]

So the model is  

\[
T(N) \;=\; 12.5\;+\;1193.5\;\frac{1}{N}.
\]

\[
\frac{1}{256}=0.00390625
\]

\begin{aligned}

       &\approx 12.5 + 4.66\\

Below is a step‑by‑step diagnosis of the bug, followed by a few clean ways to fix it, plus some extra tips (handling NaNs, normalising the weights, broadcasting safety, etc.) so the function works robustly in all realistic use‑cases.

## 1️⃣ Why the original code fails

```python
def mean_spectrum(qext, weights):
    # qext:    array (n_sizes, n_wavelengths)
    # weights: array (n_sizes,)
    weighted = qext * weights[:, None]   # shape (n_sizes, n_wavelengths)
    return np.mean(weighted) / np.mean(weights)
```

| Step | What happens | Result |
|------|--------------|--------|
| `weights[:, None]` | adds a new axis so that broadcasting works (`(n_sizes,1)`) | shape `(n_sizes,1)` |
| `qext * weights[:, None]` | element‑wise multiplication → each size gets multiplied by its weight | shape `(n_sizes, n_wavelengths)` |
| `np.mean(weighted)` | **global** mean over *all* elements (both axes) | a **scalar** |
| `np.mean(weights)` | scalar (the ordinary arithmetic mean of the weights) | scalar |
| division | scalar / scalar → scalar | **single number** |

\[
\text{mean\_spectrum}_\lambda = 
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\text{size}}} w_i \, q_{\text{ext},i,\lambda}}
     {\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\text{size}}} w_i}

    weights : ndarray, shape (n_sizes,)

    -------

    return np.average(qext, axis=0, weights=weights)

**Short answer:**  
The routine is suffering from *implicit typing* and *integer division*.  
`NSUM` is not declared, so in Fortran 77 it defaults to **INTEGER** (variables whose first letter is N‑…‑Z are integer by default).  
When you add the real elements of `X` to an integer variable the result is converted back to an integer, truncating any fractional part.  
Later the statement  

```fortran
RES = NSUM / N
```  

performs **integer‑by‑integer division**, which also truncates the fractional part (3 / 2 → 1). The integer 1 is then stored in the real variable `RES`, giving the observed result `1.0`.

---

## Step‑by‑step walk‑through of what actually happens

```fortran
SUBROUTINE MEAN(X, N, RES)
REAL X(N), RES
NSUM = 0.0                ! NSUM is an INTEGER, 0.0 is converted to 0
DO 10 I = 1, N
   NSUM = NSUM + X(I)     ! X(I) is REAL, NSUM is INTEGER
                         !   1) X(I) is promoted to REAL
                         !   2) the sum is REAL
                         !   3) the REAL result is assigned back to NSUM,
                         !      which truncates the fractional part
10 CONTINUE
RES = NSUM / N            ! Both NSUM and N are INTEGER → integer division
                         !   3 / 2 = 1 (fraction discarded)
RETURN
END
```

For the test case `X = [1.0, 2.0]` and `N = 2` the sequence of values is:

| iteration | X(I) | NSUM (INTEGER) after truncation |
|-----------|------|---------------------------------|
| start     | –    | 0                               |
| I = 1     | 1.0  | 1   (1.0 → 1)                   |
| I = 2     | 2.0  | 3   (1 + 2.0 → 3.0 → 3)          |

Then `NSUM / N` → `3 / 2` → `1` (integer division).  
`RES` receives the real value `1.0`.

---

## How to fix it

1. **Declare all variables explicitly** (or use `IMPLICIT NONE` in later standards).  
2. Make `NSUM` a `REAL`.  
3. Ensure the division is performed in real arithmetic (either by making `N` real or by converting one operand).

```fortran
      SUBROUTINE MEAN(X, N, RES)
      IMPLICIT NONE                     ! not part of Fortran‑77, but good practice
      INTEGER N, I
      REAL    X(N), RES, NSUM

      NSUM = 0.0
      DO 10 I = 1, N
         NSUM = NSUM + X(I)
10    CONTINUE

      RES = NSUM / REAL(N)              ! or RES = NSUM / N   if N is REAL
      RETURN
      END
```

If you must stay strictly within Fortran 77 syntax (no `IMPLICIT NONE`), just add the missing declarations:

```fortran
      SUBROUTINE MEAN(X, N, RES)
      REAL X(N), RES, NSUM
      INTEGER N, I
      NSUM = 0.0
      DO 10 I = 1, N
         NSUM = NSUM + X(I)
10    CONTINUE
      RES = NSUM / N
      RETURN
      END
```

Because `NSUM` is now a real variable, the addition keeps the fractional part, and the division `NSUM / N` is performed in real arithmetic (the integer `N` is automatically promoted to real). For the example `X = [1.0, 2.0]` the routine now returns `1.5`.

---

## General lessons for Fortran 77 programmers

| Issue | Symptom | Remedy |
|-------|---------|--------|
| **Implicit typing** (`IMPLICIT INTEGER (I-N)`) | Variables silently become INTEGER, leading to truncation or overflow. | Declare every variable, or add `IMPLICIT NONE` (available from Fortran 90 onward) and compile with a modern compiler that accepts it as an extension. |
| **Integer division** (`A / B` where both are INTEGER) | Fractional part is discarded. | Convert one operand to REAL (`REAL(A) / B` or `A / REAL(B)`). |
| **Assignment of REAL to INTEGER** | Fractional part lost. | Ensure the left‑hand side is REAL, or use `NINT`, `INT`, etc. |
| **Lack of `SAVE` for local arrays** (not relevant here) | Unexpected re‑initialisation on each call. | Add `SAVE` or make the array an argument. |
| **No `END SUBROUTINE` label** (optional) | Harder to match `END` with its block in long code. | Use `END SUBROUTINE MEAN` for readability. |

By following these guidelines you’ll avoid the classic “mean comes out wrong” bug and many other subtle arithmetic surprises in legacy Fortran code.

| **Mixed‑type arithmetic** | When an INTEGER and a REAL appear in the same expression, the INTEGER is **converted to REAL** (if the result type is REAL) *or* the REAL is **converted to INTEGER** (if the result type is INTEGER). | In `NSUM = NSUM + X(I)`, the left‑hand side (`NSUM`) is integer, so the right‑hand side is forced to integer → `X(I)` is truncated. |
| **Integer division** | If both operands of `/` are INTEGER, the result is INTEGER (truncation). | `NSUM/N` performed as `3/2 → 1`. |

These rules are still part of the language for backward compatibility, but they are the main source of subtle bugs in old code.

## A modern‑style rewrite (Fortran‑90/95)

If you have the luxury of moving to a newer standard, you can make the routine a bit more robust and readable:

```fortran
module stats_mod
  implicit none
contains
  subroutine mean(x, res)
    real, intent(in)  :: x(:)          ! assumed‑shape array
    real, intent(out) :: res
    real              :: nsum
    integer           :: n

    n    = size(x)
    nsum = sum(x)                     ! intrinsic sum
    res  = nsum / real(n)             ! promote n to real
  end subroutine mean
end module stats_mod
```

* `implicit none` forces explicit declarations.  
* `sum` is an intrinsic that already does the accumulation safely.  
* `real(n)` converts the integer `n` to real for the division, avoiding integer division.

Even if you must keep the original Fortran‑77 subroutine interface (because of an old library), adding `IMPLICIT NONE` and explicitly typing all locals will catch the bug at compile time.

---

## Bottom line

The routine returns the wrong answer because **`NSUM` is an INTEGER variable** and the code unintentionally performs **integer arithmetic** (truncation on each addition and integer division at the end). Declaring `NSUM` as `REAL` (or `DOUBLE PRECISION`) and, preferably, turning off implicit typing eliminates the problem.
